:::{#exm-prefix-code}
#### A prefix code and a code that is not

<!-- no-figure: the example is two small codes and their Kraft sums -->

Take four values with the codeword lengths $(1, 2, 3, 3)$.
The code $0, 10, 110, 111$ is a [prefix code](#def-prefix-code).
The code $0, 01, 011, 111$ has the same lengths,
but the codeword $0$ begins $01$, so it is not a prefix code.
The code below tests the definition on every pair of codewords,
and adds up $2^{-\ell(x)}$ for each code, as in @thm-kraft-inequality.

```{r}
#| label: prefix-code-check
is_prefix_code <- function(codewords) {
  index <- seq_along(codewords)
  pairs <- expand.grid(shorter = index, longer = index)
  distinct_pairs <- pairs[pairs$shorter != pairs$longer, ]
  shorter_words <- codewords[distinct_pairs$shorter]
  longer_words <- codewords[distinct_pairs$longer]
  begins <- startsWith(longer_words, shorter_words)
  !any(begins)
}
kraft_sum <- function(codewords) {
  lengths <- nchar(codewords)
  sum(2^(-lengths))
}
prefix_code <- c("0", "10", "110", "111")
other_code <- c("0", "01", "011", "111")
codes <- list(prefix_code, other_code)
data.frame(
  code = c("0, 10, 110, 111", "0, 01, 011, 111"),
  is_prefix_code = vapply(codes, is_prefix_code, logical(1)),
  kraft_sum = vapply(codes, kraft_sum, numeric(1))
)
```

Both codes have $\sum_x 2^{-\ell(x)} = `r kraft_sum(prefix_code)`$,
so Kraft's inequality holds with equality for the lengths $(1, 2, 3, 3)$.
The inequality is a condition on the lengths alone,
so it holds for the second code even though the second code is not a prefix code;
@thm-kraft-converse says that a prefix code with these lengths exists,
and the first code is one.

:::
